  MISSION STATEMENT
  The mission of the City of Monterey Park is to provide excellent service, foster growth
  and opportunity, and create a joyous and collaborative environment.

  LAND ACKNOWLEDGMENT
  We would like to acknowledge that the land we inhabit today was once known as
  Tovangaar, the home of the Gabrieleño-Tongva people. We show our respect to the
  Gabrieleño-Tongva people, as well as all Indigenous people, past, present, and future,
  and honor their labor as original caretakers of this land. We commit to uplifting the
  Gabrieleño-Tongva people, invite you to acknowledge the history, and join us in caring
  for this land.

GENERAL INFORMATION
Documents related to an Agenda item are available to the public in the City Clerk’s Office located at 320
West Newmark Avenue, Monterey Park, CA 91754, during normal business hours and the City’s website
at http://www.montereypark.ca.gov/AgendaCenter/City-Council-17.

The public may watch the meeting live on the city’s cable channel MPKTV (AT&T U-verse, channel 99
or Charter Communications, channel 182) or by visiting the city’s website at
http://www.montereypark.ca.gov/133/City-Council-Meeting-Videos. Per the Americans with Disabilities
Act, if you need special assistance to participate in this meeting, please call City Hall at (626) 307-1359
for reasonable accommodation at least 24 hours before a meeting. Council Chambers are wheelchair
accessible.

PUBLIC PARTICIPATION
You may speak up to 5 minutes on an/each Agenda item. You may combine up to 2 minutes of time with
another person’s speaking. No person may speak more than a total of 10 minutes. The Mayor and City
Council may change the amount of time allowed for speakers. Written Communication will be accepted
up to 24 hours before the meeting via email to mpclerk@montereypark.ca.gov or by completing an online
form at www.montereypark.ca.gov/writtencomm.

While all comments are welcome, the Brown Act does not allow the City Council to take action on any
item not on the agenda. The Council may briefly respond to comments after Public Communications is
closed. Persons may, in addition to any other matter within the City Council's subject-matter jurisdiction,
comment on Agenda Items at this time. If you provide public comment on a specific Agenda item at this
time, however, you cannot later provide comments at the time the Agenda Item is considered.

 TO:  The Honorable Mayor and City Council
 FROM:  Diana Garcia, Assistant City Manager
 SUBJECT:  Update on the Work of the January 21 Memorial Ad Hoc Subcommittee
  and Consideration of Further Action

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Receiving and filing this report on the permanent memorial process;
  2. Providing further direction to staff on next steps; and
  3. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
The January 21 Memorial Ad Hoc Subcommittee made progress in exploring options for
a permanent memorial to honor the victims of the 2023 mass shooting and learning more
about how other communities affected by mass violence have addressed this important
work. Staff is updating Council on the progress of the Subcommittee and asking for further
direction from City Council on next steps.

BACKGROUND:
In response to the tragic mass shooting on January 21, 2023, which claimed 11 lives, the
City of Monterey Park has worked to support the community’s mental health and healing
in variety of ways, from providing support and counseling in City facilities, to assisting with
the opening of the MPK Hope Resiliency Center and the establishment of the MPK
Healing Fund, to holding events to bring community members together to remember and
honor victims and survivors.

Since the shooting, the City has also considered the establishment a permanent memorial
to honor the victims and support community healing.

  Ø Preliminary Research and the First 12 Months

At the City Council meeting on September 6, 2023, in order to help guide initial discussion
and inform any next steps the Council was provided with preliminary research on
memorials for six mass casualty events in the United States: Sandy Hook Elementary
School (Sandy Hook, Connecticut), Route 91 Harvest Music Festival (Las Vegas,
Nevada), Inland Regional Center Attack (San Bernardino, California), Borderline Bar and

  Page 5 of 394
 Staff Report
Page 2 of 4
January 15, 2025

Grill Shooting (Thousand Oaks, CA), PULSE Nightclub (Orlando, Florida), and the
Virginia Tech Shooting (Blacksburg, Virginia) .

The City Council initially considered the six different memorial committees, their
composition, methods of community input, responsibilities, timelines and budgets. At that
point, the discussion was preliminary, as mass casualty experts that staff had consulted
with advised that it was very early in the healing process to begin to make decisions on a
permanent memorial.

On January 21, 2024, the City held a vigil to mark one year since the shooting and to
allow the community to come together in unity and support. The event incorporated
Buddhist chanting, prayer, a Tongva blessing, music from Mark Keppel’s string quintet,
and remarks from City of Monterey Park elected officials, and survivors, family and
community members. The City has a vigil to mark the second year since the shooting
scheduled for January 21, 2025 at 6:00 p.m. in front of Monterey Park City Hall.

  Ø Council-Established Ad Hoc Subcommittee

In May 2024, staff brought the permanent memorial discussion back to City Council, and
an ad hoc subcommittee to further consider the issue of a permanent memorial in
Monterey Park was established. The subcommittee is comprised of two members of the
City Council: Mayor Thomas Wong and Councilmember Henry Lo.

Since its establishment, the subcommittee, along with City Manager Inez Alvarez and
Assistant City Manager Diana Garcia, has met with individuals who have personal
experience setting up memorials in the aftermath of mass casualty incidents, including
Tennille Pereira, who has worked to support the community in the aftermath of the Route
91 shooting in Las Vegas and Anita Ahuja, who has helped communities respond to mass
violence for over twenty years. The subcommittee has considered various topics
associated with the establishment of a memorial, including funding, outreach and
communication, staffing, committee composition, professional facilitators, memorial
design, request for proposal processes, and project timelines.

  Ø Partnership with Chinatown Service Center

Since the mass shooting, City staff has worked closely with the Chinatown Service Center
(CSC) to support the community’s healing. In September 2024, Nina Loc, CSC’s Chief
Behavioral Health Officer and then Director of the MPK Hope Resiliency Center, informed
staff that CSC was initiating discussions with the family members of victims and the
survivors about their sentiments on a permanent memorial. As a part of this feedback
process CSC staff also created a survey to gather additional feedback from victims and
survivors about the permanent memorial.

After approximately three months of discussions and surveying the family members and
survivors, CSC staff pushed the survey out in January 2025 to the greater community to

  Page 6 of 394
 Staff Report
Page 3 of 4
January 15, 2025

gather input. This survey will run through the end of February 2025. The City has shared
the survey via social media, the City website, and promotion in our City facilities, and will
distribute paper survey at the Bruggemeyer Library and the Langley Senior Center.

Initial survey results indicate a general interest in establishing a memorial, though 5% of
respondents indicated that they are "uncertain", and another 5% are "not interested” in
establishing a memorial. Respondent largely support an outdoor garden memorial, or a
mural, memorial wall or sculpture.

  Ø Next Steps

In cities affected by mass casualty events, outreach efforts to establish a permanent
memorial—such as surveys, meetings, and town hall events—are often led by Resiliency
Center staff who maintain close ties to the impacted communities. These efforts help
ensure that the memorial reflects the desires and needs of those most affected.

In Monterey Park, staff from the MPK Hope Resiliency Center are continuing to survey
residents through at least February 2025 to gauge interest and gather input on the
potential establishment of a permanent memorial. City staff are currently assisting in
promoting this survey to ensure broad community participation.

Subcommittee and staff recommend that the City Council provide direction on the next
steps in this process. Possible options include:

  •  Allowing Additional Outreach: Waiting until outreach efforts are concluded to
  gain further input from the community.
  •  Designating a Memorial Committee: Provide direction regarding the creation of
  a committee; or delegation of oversight to members of the City Council or other
  entity.
  •  Dedicating City Property: Identifying and dedicating a City property or space for
  a memorial.
  •  Fundraising Efforts: Directing a designated entity to initiate fundraising for the
  memorial with a set timeframe for these efforts and based on funds collected
  establish next steps.

FISCAL IMPACT:
There is no immediate fiscal impact associated with this discussion.

  DATE: September 6, 2023

 TO:  The Honorable Mayor and City Council
 FROM:  Inez Alvarez, Interim City Manager
 SUBJECT:  Discussion of Establishing a Memorial Committee for the January 21st
  Mass Shooting Incident

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Receiving and filing the staff report and attachments;
  2. Discussing the establishment an independent Memorial Committee for the January
  21st Mass Shooting Incident;
  3. If desirable, providing additional staff direction; and
  4. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
On January 21st, the City of Monterey Park experienced a tragic mass shooting incident
that resulted in the loss of 11 lives and left the community deeply affected. The City
recognizes the need to honor the memory of the victims and create a space for healing,
remembrance, and reflection for the entire community.

In response to this tragic event, there has been public interest and support for the creation
of a permanent memorial that will serve as a place for residents and visitors to pay their
respects and remember the lives that were lost. The memorial would serve not only as a
tribute to the victims but also as a symbol of resilience and unity for the Monterey Park
community. Communities affected by similar tragedies often establish committees that
tackle the fundraising, outreach and planning for permanent memorials, which consist of
a diverse group of community members, stakeholders, and experts in memorial design
and public spaces.

Initial research on the memorials for six mass casualty events in the United States is
attached for Council to review and to help guide initial discussion. Council may provide
direction on next steps and/or request this item to be put on the agenda for discussion at
future meetings.

BACKGROUND:
Other communities affected by mass violence have formed commissions to establish
permanent memorials to their victims. Attachment 1 outlines staff’s initial research on the
processes undertaken in response to six tragedies: Sandy Hook Elementary School

  Page 10 of 394
 Staff Report
Page 2 of 4
September 6, 2023

processes undertaken in response to six tragedies: Sandy Hook Elementary School
(Sandy Hook, Connecticut), Route 91 Harvest Music Festival (Las Vegas, Nevada),
Inland Regional Center Attack (San Bernardino, California), Borderline Bar and Grill
Shooting (Thousand Oaks, CA), PULSE Nightclub (Orlando, Florida), and the Virginia
Tech Shooting (Blacksburg, Virginia). This table includes the composition of the
committees; the timelines for the establishment of the committees and the completion
date of the memorial; the outreach and methodologies used by each committee to gather
input from the community; the budget for the projects; and additional information on the
processes.

This information is provided to illustrate the potential budgets, timelines and
considerations that Council may want to contemplate as they begin to consider how best
to move forward. While some communities have established memorials within a matter
of months, others have taken years. The memorial in Sandy Hook, Connecticut for
example took nearly 10 years to complete. Accordingly, the budgets for memorials vary
from $70,000 for the Virginia Tech memorial to $10 million for the PULSE nightclub
memorial and museum. The average cost for the six examples is $4.25 million. Any
potential Memorial Committee to investigate these topics, as well as the planning, design,
and implementation of the official memorial to honor the victims of the January 21st
shooting.

Additional items for consideration for a potential Memorial Committee may include:

Name of the Committee: Establish a name for the Memorial Committee.

Committee Members: Identify how many committee members would be appropriate and
identify potential persons to serve on the committee, which may include a variety of
community members, commissioners, stakeholders, patrons/survivors from the incident,
family members of the victims, and/or other appropriate persons that will represent a
diverse and inclusive group.

Committee Roles and Responsibilities: Determine roles and items that the committee
will be responsible for undertaking, which may include some the of the categories listed
below or others identified:

Location Selection: Identify potential locations within the city for the memorial and
assess their feasibility, accessibility, and appropriateness for the intended purpose.

Conceptualization and Design: Work collaboratively to develop conceptual designs for
the memorial, considering input from the community, victim families, and experts in public
spaces and memorials. Or will there be an open RFP process to allow for concept
submissions by design contractors.

  Page 11 of 394
 Staff Report
Page 3 of 4
September 6, 2023

Community Engagement: Facilitate public input and engagement sessions to gather
input from residents, victim families, and other stakeholders regarding the design,
features, and significance of the memorial.

Budgeting and Fundraising: Review established permanent memorials in other
locations that have experienced mass casualty events. Analyze their budgeting and
fundraising strategies, taking note of community partnerships and sources of funding.

Timeline: Study the timelines of memorial development in those aforementioned
locations, examining the phases of conceptualization, design, approvals, construction,
and dedication.

Partnerships: Explore potential partnerships with local organizations, businesses, and
nonprofits that may offer support, resources, or expertise in memorial development.

Process Documentation: Develop a comprehensive process outline for the
establishment of the memorial, considering lessons learned from other memorial projects.

Community Updates: Identify how often the Committee should be providing an update.

2023-2024 STRATEGIC PLAN GOAL:
This action helps meet the MPK Healing 2023-24 goal of “providing community support
resulting from the shooting incident”.

FISCAL IMPACT:
There is no immediate fiscal impact associated with this discussion.

 SUBJECT:  Establishing an Ad Hoc Subcommittee of the City Council to Discuss the
  Creation of an independent Memorial Committee for the January 21,
  2023 Mass Casualty Incident

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Establishing an ad hoc subcommittee comprised of two members of the City
  Council which will appoint and give initial direction to an independent Memorial
  Committee for the January 21, 2023 Mass Casualty Incident; and
  2. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
On January 21, 2023, the City of Monterey Park suffered a mass casualty incident that
resulted in the loss of 11 lives, nine injured individuals, and left the community deeply
affected. The City recognizes the need to honor the memory of the victims and create a
space for healing and remembrance for the entire community.

Communities affected by similar tragedies often establish committees consisting of a
diverse group of community members and stakeholders which consider the fundraising,
location, community input and planning for permanent memorials.

The City Manager is proposing the establishment of an ad hoc subcommittee of two City
Council members. This ad hoc subcommittee will be tasked with appointing members to
a January 21 Memorial Committee and providing initial direction on the roles and
responsibilities of the Memorial Committee, as well as the method and frequency by which
the Committee should report to the City Council on its progress.

BACKGROUND:
Many communities affected by mass violence have formed committees to establish
permanent memorials to honor victims and survivors. Because each community has its
own unique set of circumstances, each memorial committee has different factors,
considerations and issues to consider as it plans for a permanent memorial space. In
addition, committee members will need to be advised that the completion of a memorial
project can take several years to create as many factors must be taken into consideration
when establishing a memorial representative of the impacted community. At the
September 6, 2023 meeting, City Council was provided with research on six different

memorial committees, their composition, methods of community input, responsibilities,
timelines and budgets. This staff report and research is included as Attachment 1.

In order to begin exploring the creation of a permanent memorial to honor the victims and
survivors of the January 21, 2023 mass shooting in Monterey Park, the City Council may
consider forming a temporary subcommittee comprised of two City Council members.
This subcommittee's purpose will be to select individuals for a Memorial Committee and
to offer initial guidance on the duties and functions of the Memorial Committee, including
how often the Committee should update the City Council on its activities. Additionally, the
ad hoc subcommittee may wish to consider the following issues and responsibilities as it
establishes a January 21 Memorial Committee:

  1. Composition
  The Memorial Committee may consist of a diverse group of community members,
  stakeholders, survivors, family members of victims, and experts in memorial
  design and public spaces. The committee should represent the demographics and
  interests of not only the Monterey Park community but also the regional community
  that was impacted by this tragedy.

  2. Roles and Objectives
  The committee may be tasked with:
  • Selecting an appropriate name for the memorial committee.
  • Deciding when and how often to meet.
  • Identifying potential locations within the city for the memorial and assessing
  their feasibility, accessibility, and appropriateness.
  • Developing conceptual designs for the memorial in collaboration with the
  community members, stakeholders, survivors, victim families, and design
  experts.
  • Facilitating public engagement sessions to gather input on the design and
  significance of the memorial.
  • Researching budgeting and fundraising strategies employed by other
  memorial projects and identifying potential sources of funding.
  • Establishing a timeline for the various phases of memorial development,
  including conceptualization, design, approvals, construction, and
  dedication.
  • Exploring partnerships with local organizations, businesses, and nonprofits
  to support the memorial project.

  3. Reporting Frequency
  The January 21 Memorial Committee will provide regular updates to the City
  Council on its progress and activities. The frequency of these updates will be
  determined by the ad hoc subcommittee, with consideration given to the
  milestones and timelines established for the memorial project.

 SUBJECT:  Discussion of Findings on City’s Updated Inclusionary Housing
  Ordinance Feasibility/Fee Study

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Receiving and filing the report and presentation;
  2. Providing direction to staff; and
  3. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
On September 6, 2023, the City Council adopted an Inclusionary Housing Ordinance
("IHO”) and an in-lieu fee formula to encourage affordable housing in Monterey Park. The
Council also directed the City Manager to assess the IHO’s financial feasibility and
recommend in-lieu fees where necessary. To assist in this evaluation, the City partnered
with the San Gabriel Valley Council of Governments (“SGVCOG”) and engaged
Economic & Planning Systems (“EPS”) for a tailored feasibility study.

On January 17, 2024, the feasibility study was presented to City Council and found that
the IHO's requirements could present financial challenges for new residential projects,
particularly smaller and mid-sized developments. Based on this analysis, the City Council
directed staff to pause enforcement of the IHO for one year and revisit its financial
feasibility in the coming year.

EPS was hired to review the previously prepared feasibility study and update it to reflect
current market conditions. In updating the feasibility study, during the Council-directed
IHO enforcement pause, EPS looked at both direct and indirect factors that may change
the financial feasibility of implementing the IHO. The study’s overall conclusion states that
while the requirements of the IHO are likely to remain financially challenging for new
residential development within the City and may constrain new projects, current market
conditions have demonstrated improved feasibility of new residential projects overall
since the previous analysis.

BACKGROUND:
The City adopted the 2021-2029 Housing Element of the General Plan on January 19,
2022; it was certified by the California Department of Housing and Community
Development on March 20, 2023. Housing Element Program 15 provides that the City
Council will consider an inclusionary housing program. Such programs require certain
residential and mixed-use developments to designate a percentage of units within the
development as affordable housing. Alternatively, a developer may construct off-site
units, or pay a fee or dedicate land in the City for the creation of affordable units.

To implement Program 15 of the Housing Element, the Council began consideration of
an IHO in Fall of 2022. The IHO was ultimately approved on September 6, 2023. Along
with the IHO, a formula for calculating an in-lieu fee was adopted for developers who opt
to pay a fee, rather than construct units on-site was also adopted. This formula requires
the developer to pay the “affordability gap,” which represents the gap between the market-
rate price (sales or rent) and the affordable price (sales or rent) of the inclusionary unit.

EPS was hired to review the previously prepared feasibility study and update it to reflect
current market conditions. EPS drew on local research and input from City
representatives, revisited the building prototypes representative of development patterns
in the City, and assessed how the City’s IHO and in-lieu fee formula would affect the
different prototype developments.

The assessment utilized data on typical construction and land costs and rents and sales
prices for recently-built housing projects in the City and in the larger San Gabriel Valley
subregion. Additionally, EPS factored in policy changes that affect the development costs
of projects. Specifically, the City updated parking requirements in multi-family residential
developments in October of 2024, which requires less parking in multi-family residential
projects, and subsequently lowers the cost of construction.

The data allowed EPS to evaluate how likely a developer would be to pursue the
construction of the modeled prototypes, based on industry standard financial feasibility
metrics. The evaluation modeled the financial feasibility for the prototypes under three
different assumptions:

  1. That they are rented or sold completely at market rents/sale prices;
  2. That they include the affordable units required by the IHO; and
  3. That they pay an in-lieu fee aligned with the requirements of the IHO (i.e., based
  on the “affordability gap”).

The findings of the analysis generally indicate that the financial impacts of the City’s IHO
and in-lieu fee formula may dampen new residential development in the City.

City Council may consider one or a combination of the following next steps:
  - Phase-in inclusionary requirements over a period of time
  - Reinstate the inclusionary housing policy for ownership prototypes only

The City of Monterey Park (City) engaged Economic & Planning
Systems, Inc. (EPS) to conduct an update to its feasibility
analysis of the City’s Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (IHO). EPS
previously conducted a feasibility study of the City’s IHO in late
2023, and this update aligns with the City Council’s decision at
that time to pause implementation of the IHO for 12 months and
reassess its feasibility in early 2025. In the current analysis, EPS
updated assumptions regarding the analyzed residential
prototype products, including using cost and revenue
assumptions that reflect current market conditions, as follows:

Development Program Updates:

•  With the City’s newly approved minimum parking
  requirements, all prototypes are assumed to have one
  parking space per unit, except the townhome prototype,
  which still has two parking spaces.

•  For the condominium prototype in the Mixed-Use zoning
  area, the current analysis increases the density to 70
  dwelling units per acre from 30 dwelling units per acre.

Cost and Revenue Updates:

•  Construction costs are assumed to remain the same.

•  Land acquisition costs increased.

•  Rent and sales price for all prototypes increased, except for
  the townhome prototypes, for which the sales price remained
  constant.

The key findings and recommendations stemming from the updated feasibility analysis
are summarized below.

1. The financial feasibility of residential projects improved from 2023 analysis
  due to changes in market conditions and reduced parking requirements. All
  residential prototypes yielded an improved feasibility, with the exception of the
  townhome prototype. The City’s reduced parking requirements was a major driver in
  reducing overall development costs. Additionally, increases in market rent and sales
  price resulted in increased prototype value. These changes resulted in improved
  feasibility despite assumed increases in land costs increasing. Townhome prototype
  feasibility did not improve because the parking requirement and sales price
  assumptions for the prototype stayed constant, while land costs increased.

2. Renter-occupied residential projects continue to appear financially
  challenging to build in the City, while owner-occupied projects appear
  financially feasible. Although the feasibility of developing of rental residential
  products improved since the 2023 analysis, the analysis indicates that these products,
  in both Mixed-Use zoned areas and Citywide, appear financially infeasible on average
  at market rates. By contrast, owner-occupied attached townhomes and multifamily
  condominiums appear to be feasible at market rates, and demonstrate sufficient
  development feasibility to absorb the additional impact of an inclusionary
  requirement, specifically townhomes and higher density condominiums in the Mixed-
  Use zone. Condominiums outside the Mixed-Use zone seem to be feasible at market
  rates, but may not be feasible with the addition of inclusionary requirements.

3. The zoning allowances under the City’s Mixed-Use zoning designation may
  improve the financial feasibility of residential projects. Residential projects in
  the Mixed-Use zoned areas of the City generate a higher return on investment than
  development in other parts of the City due to the Mixed-Use zone’s unlimited density
  allowances. However, in order for future projects in the Mixed-Use zone to support
  the additional cost of inclusionary units, they would likely need to achieve even higher
  densities than what is proposed for current pipeline projects.

4. Although feasibility improved across most residential prototypes since the
  2023 analysis, not all prototype products demonstrated enough feasibility to
  support an inclusionary housing policy. To improve the efficacy of the IHO in
  developing affordable units in the community while also supporting new residential
  development overall, the City may consider one or a combination of the following
  next steps:

  o  Phase-in inclusionary requirements over a period of time
  o  Reinstate the inclusionary housing policy for ownership prototypes only
  o  Adjust IHO requirements such that rental projects automatically qualify for
  State Density Bonus
  o  Adopt an in-lieu fee at a level that is lower than the equivalent of providing
  units on-site, knowing that developers will opt to pay the fee
  o  Continue to pause some or all inclusionary requirements and reassess in the
  next one to two years as market conditions change

1. Introduction

Study Background
The City of Monterey Park (City) adopted an Inclusionary Housing Ordinance
(IHO) in August 2023 and it became effective in September 2023. Inclusionary
housing ordinances require that new market-rate residential development projects
include a certain percentage of housing units at rents or sale prices that are
affordable to lower-income households. Per the City’s IHO, developers of new
residential projects are required to provide 15 percent of the new units built as
affordable to lower-income households. For rental developments, the 15 percent
requirement consists of 9 percent of units affordable to households earning the
Low-Income level for Los Angeles County and 6 percent of units affordable to
households earning the Moderate Income level. For ownership developments, 15
percent of units are required to be affordable to households earning the Moderate
Income level. 1 The IHO also includes an option for developers to pay a fee in-lieu
of providing affordable units on-site as an alternative means of compliance.

Following adoption of the IHO, the City sought to study how the ordinance could
impact the financial feasibility of new market-rate housing developments in the
City. Additionally, the City wanted to consider a more standardized and
transparent approach to the in-lieu fee formula included in the IHO. The current
formula requires the developer to uniquely calculate the gap between the value of
their project’s market-rate units and the value of the required affordable units,
and leaves room for interpretation regarding the calculation of unit value, which
can fluctuate on a variety of factors such as unit size, type, market conditions,
and more.

Economic & Planning Systems, Inc. (EPS) was retained by the San Gabriel Valley
Council of Governments (SGVCOG) on behalf of the City to conduct a feasibility
analysis of the IHO and to calculate potential in-lieu fee levels that are consistent
with the IHO’s on-site unit requirement. The feasibility analysis specifically tests
whether new market-rate residential developments in the City can absorb the
additional financial costs associated with the IHO requirements and still be
financially feasible. While cities are generally not legally required to consider the
financial impacts of an inclusionary housing requirement, the City has elected
to study them to better inform its inclusionary housing policy and align the City’s
overall housing goals with its local real estate market conditions. 2

Overview of Feasibility Analysis
The financial feasibility of a development project is determined by comparing the
cost of the project to its value (based on achievable sale prices or rents).
A financially feasible project is one in which the value provides a sufficient return
on the investment to incentivize moving forward with the project. Given the range
of investment opportunities available to developers and financial investors,
a development project will not be built if it is not considered a financially feasible
proposition. For the purposes of this study’s analysis, a “sufficient” return on
investment was established using market-based standards that are relevant
at the time of this analysis (further detailed in Chapter 3). However, what is
considered a “sufficient” return for any individual project will vary depending on
a range of considerations.

The impacts of inclusionary housing policies on the financial feasibility of market-
rate housing projects can manifest in one of two ways:

1. On-site inclusionary affordable units typically cost the same to build as the
  market-rate units but are sold or rented at below-market rates; OR
2. Fees paid in-lieu of providing affordable units on-site add to the costs of a
  project, while the value of the project as reflected in market-rate rents or sale
  prices tends to stay the same.

The resulting decrease in project revenue or increase in development costs
related to inclusionary policies will reduce the achievable return on investment for
housing projects. At a certain level, the impacts of the policy may reduce the
achievable return to the point that projects are financially infeasible, and
developers will not move forward with building them. This study is intended to
provide the City with additional context regarding the cost associated with its
inclusionary requirement and whether it might render new residential
development in the City extremely challenging or even completely financially
infeasible. This context is important given that the production of affordable units
through an inclusionary housing policy can only happen through the development
of larger market-rate projects.

Key Findings and Recommendations
The key findings and recommendations stemming from the feasibility analysis for
inclusionary housing in Monterey Park are summarized below. It is important to
note that the analysis is a point-in-time assessment of typical new market-rate
development projects completed in late 2023. The findings are not deterministic
of all development feasibility in the City, as there are many variables that can
impact costs and values and resulting feasibility of any individual project.
Similarly, future market conditions can also change the financial forces impacting
real estate development generally and inclusionary housing programs specifically.

1. Higher-density owner- and renter-occupied residential projects
  appear financially challenging to build in the City, while lower-density
  owner-occupied projects appear financially feasible. The feasibility
  analysis indicates that the development of higher density residential products,
  such as multifamily owner-occupied condominiums and renter-occupied
  apartments, appear financially infeasible even at market rates. By contrast,
  lower density residential products such as owner-occupied attached
  townhomes appears to be feasible at market rates, and demonstrate sufficient
  development feasibility to absorb the additional impact of an inclusionary
  requirement.

2. The zoning allowances under the City’s Mixed-Use (MU) zoning
  designation may improve the financial feasibility of residential
  projects. Residential projects in the MU zoned areas of the City generate a
  higher return on investment than development in other parts of the City due
  to the MU zone’s unlimited density allowances and lower parking
  requirements. However, in order for future projects in the MU zone to support
  the additional cost of inclusionary units, they would likely need to achieve
  even higher densities and lower parking ratios than the MU pipeline projects
  currently proposed.

3. The City’s current inclusionary housing requirements will likely be
  financially challenging for new residential development projects under
  current market conditions. This challenge is particularly seen for
  multifamily residential rental and ownership projects, which are facing other
  financial challenges related to development costs and achievable market
  rates. Chapter 5 of this report outlines a number of options the City may
  consider to improve the efficacy of the IHO in developing affordable units in
  the community while also supporting new residential development overall.

The subsequent chapters of this report detail on the methodology, key
assumptions, and results of the feasibility analysis, as well as the calculation of an
in-lieu fee aligned with the City’s current IHO requirements.

3. Development Feasibility Analysis
The development feasibility analysis detailed in this study tests whether new
market-rate residential development in the City can absorb the financial impact of
an inclusionary housing requirement. This assessment reflects that building
affordable housing units represents a cost to market-rate housing projects, and it
is possible that the additional cost will cause the project to be financially
infeasible.

Methodology
To support an inclusionary requirement, a development project must demonstrate
feasibility in excess of a feasibility “threshold,” described in more detail below.
Based on this criterion, the feasibility analysis is intended to demonstrate if an
inclusionary housing program is an appropriate tool to adopt at this time given
market conditions, and, if so, identify inclusionary requirements that could be
feasibly absorbed by different types of new market-rate projects in the City. The
analysis utilizes information on market rents and sale prices in the City, affordable
rents and sale prices in the region, and development costs for new residential
units in the region. The analysis reflects costs and values of newly constructed
housing units since the IHO only applies to new development projects.

Assumptions
Product Prototypes
The feasibility analysis was conducted on a series of prototype residential
products intended to reflect the types of new residential development projects
expected to occur in the City in the coming years. The prototypes were informed
by EPS research on the local housing market, which included review of recent
developments and proposed projects, discussions with developers active in the
City and subregion, input from City staff, and City zoning regulations.

The analyzed prototypes include three Citywide prototypes, reflecting residential
zoning designations across the City; and three MU Zone prototypes reflecting the
City’s MU zoning designation. Prototypes for the MU Zone are considered
separately as the MU designation provides zoning allowances distinct from other
residential zones in the City. Specifically, there is no limit on density for projects
in the MU Zone. Additionally, many of the properties located in the MU Zone meet
the requirements of California law, which allows a developer to provide fewer
parking spaces than required by the City standards if the development is
constructed within ½ miles of a major transit hub. Since the MU Zone is expected
to absorb a significant amount of future residential development in the City, it is

The Citywide prototypes include one rental prototype – multifamily apartments –

how the lot is subdivided – that the City uses to define a project as a
condominium or townhome, this analysis does not account for those types of
factors and only differentiates the prototypes based on density and unit size.

The Mixed-Use prototypes include two rental multifamily apartment prototypes
and one for-sale multifamily condominium prototype. These products reflect
characteristics of pipeline projects currently seen in the MU Zone. The difference

Value Assumptions
Market-Rate Residential Values
The value for market-rate rental apartments is based on annual net operating
income (NOI), which is calculated as annual rent minus annual operating
expenses. For the apartment prototypes in Monterey Park, annual rent is assumed
at $33,420 per unit (equivalent to $2,785 per month), and annual operating
expenses are assumed at $10,000 per unit. This rental rate reflects market rents
for newly constructed apartment projects in the San Gabriel Valley subregion.

For the market-rate for-sale prototypes, the value of the unit is equal to the
estimated sale price. The assumed price points for new for-sale products in
Monterey Park are $674,000 for a condominium unit and $870,000 for a
townhome unit. These price points reflect expectations for newly constructed
units, which are assumed to achieve higher prices than the overall existing
inventory. For this analysis, EPS applied a premium of 40 percent over existing
inventory values to estimate projected prices for new units, based on sales trend
data for the San Gabriel Valley subregion.

Affordable Residential Values
Affordable rents and sale prices for inclusionary units are based on maximum
housing costs affordable to households at various household income levels.
Income levels for households in Los Angeles County are set by California law on
an annual basis. The income level for each category differs by household size.
This analysis assumes a two-bedroom unit is occupied by a three-person
household and a three-bedroom unit is occupied by a four-person household. 8 For
2023, the Area Median Income (AMI) in Los Angeles County is defined as $88,400
for a household of three and $98,200 for a household of four.

In general, Very Low-Income households are defined as those earning up to
50 percent of AMI; Low-Income households earn up to 80 percent AMI; and
Moderate-Income households earn up to 120 percent of AMI. However, within
Los Angeles County, the maximum income defining Very Low- and Low-Income
households is adjusted upwards from the associated percentage of AMI. This
adjustment occurs in counties with relatively high housing costs and/or relatively
high or low household incomes. Due to this adjustment, the maximum income for

Feasibility Thresholds
The assessment of financial feasibility for real estate development products is
based on calculating financial return metrics for the products and comparing them
against typical industry target thresholds. In the case of residential development,
relevant return metrics are based on comparing total project revenues to total
project development costs, as follows:

•  For for-sale market-rate housing prototypes, which in this analysis includes
  condominiums and townhomes, the estimated cost of development (shown in
  Table 5, Table 6, and Table 9) is subtracted from the estimated value, or
  sale price, in order to calculate profit. The profit is then divided by the
  estimated development cost to calculate the relevant feasibility metric, profit
  margin, which is the percentage by which total project value exceeds total
  project cost. Based on EPS research and feedback from the developer
  community, the analysis assumes that developers in the greater Los Angeles
  region will require a projected profit margin of at least 15 percent to move
  forward with a for-sale development project. Therefore, a prototype attaining
  a profit margin at or above 15 percent at market sale prices would be
  considered feasible in this analysis. A profit margin in excess of 15 percent
  would be required to support any additional costs, such as an inclusionary
  requirement.

•  For rental market-rate housing prototypes, which in this analysis includes
  multifamily apartments, the feasibility threshold is based on the return metric
  of “yield on cost,” which is calculated by dividing the annual net operating
  income (NOI) by the total costs of development. 9 Based on EPS research and
  experience, the analysis assumes that developers in the greater Los Angeles
  region will require a projected yield on cost of at least 5.5 percent in order to
  move forward with a multifamily rental development project. A yield-on-cost
  in excess of 5.5 percent would be required to support any additional costs,
  such as an inclusionary requirement.

It is important to note that these return metrics do not account for the time value
of money and are not based on any assumption regarding project timeline.

EPS assumptions for prototype revenues and costs detailed above were used to

As shown, the analysis indicates that only the townhome prototype both meets

support the additional costs of an inclusionary requirement. None of the
multifamily prototypes achieve feasible return thresholds at market rates,
although the Mixed-Use prototypes’ higher densities and lower parking ratios
increase revenue and lower development cost, and are therefore estimated to
generate higher returns as compared to their Citywide counterparts. Overall, the
estimated returns for the multifamily prototypes suggest that, on average, it is
challenging to develop these project types in the City under current market
conditions. The additional costs of an inclusionary requirement would exacerbate
those challenges and potentially limit the opportunities for new housing
development in the community.

It is important to note that this analysis only reflects average prototypical projects
and does not mean that the prototypes shown as infeasible above will never be
built in the City. There are many factors that can impact the financial feasibility of
any particular development project. For example, if a project can acquire land at a
lower price or build at a higher density than what is represented in the above
assumptions, the project may become financially feasible. Similarly, a developer
may find that there is sufficient demand to achieve rents or sale prices higher
than those assumed in this analysis. Indeed, the City may find that even though
this analysis shows specific types of development to be infeasible at market rates,
they still receive proposals to build these types of projects. Therefore, as stated
previously in this report, the analysis should not be considered deterministic
regarding the future of housing development in the City. Rather, it should be
taken as informative regarding the obstacles to housing development under
current average market conditions, and how inclusionary housing requirements
might therefore impact the feasibility of the average project.

4. In-Lieu Fee Calculation
In addition to evaluating the impacts of the City’s IHO on development feasibility,
EPS was scoped to calculate an in-lieu fee that developers might pay instead of
providing affordable units on-site. The City adopted a resolution in September
2023 regarding calculation of the in-lieu fee, which called for the fee to equal “the
difference between the market rate price and the defined affordable price…
associated with each income restricted unit required to be produced.”10 While this
is one possible approach for calculating an in-lieu fee, EPS recommends an
alternative approach that would still reflect the City’s goal to establish a fee that
reflects “the financial impact or ‘affordability gap’ that is created by the IHO,” and
is commonly used in other jurisdictions across the State. 11

In EPS’s recommended approach, the in-lieu fee is set to equal (as closely as
possible) the cost that developers incur in providing on-site affordable units. This
cost manifests as a “financial gap” associated with inclusionary units, calculated
as the cost of developing the inclusionary unit (which is the same as the cost to
build a market-rate unit) minus the inclusionary unit’s value based on maximum
affordable rents or sales prices. The in-lieu fee per required affordable unit would
be based on that financial gap.

Using the financial gap approach described above, EPS calculated the financial
gap for each modeled prototype unit at values associated with Low- and
Moderate-Income affordability levels. The calculation utilizes the development
costs detailed in Table 4 through Table 9 and affordable rents and sale prices
detailed in Table 10. These gaps are shown in Table 12 below.

Given these findings, EPS has outlined several strategies for the City to consider
regarding the immediate and long-term future of the IHO. These strategies can
help the City balance its affordable housing objectives with current market and
development feasibility conditions. These strategies are not necessarily mutually
exclusive, and the City may decide to pursue them in combination.

1. Temporarily pause the inclusionary housing requirement. The City may
  consider a pause in enforcement of the IHO until there is more market
  evidence that the development economics of residential development,
  particularly multifamily development, are improving. The City can continue to
  monitor several metrics in this regard, including developer interest and
  applications, residential production trends, development costs, and market
  prices/rents in the City. A reasonable timeframe for monitoring changing real
  estate and financial markets conditions would be one to two years. When
  early indicators, such as increased developer interest and multifamily rents,
  suggest improving market conditions, the City may then reevaluate the
  feasibility of its inclusionary program. While it would be a “best practice” to
  conduct another feasibility study at that time, the law does not require it.

2. Phase-in the IHO requirements. It can take some time for the market to
  respond to new inclusionary requirements and for developers to figure out
  how to adjust their development programs to maintain feasibility. Sometimes
  phasing in inclusionary requirements is a way for a jurisdiction to signal to the
  development community what is coming while allowing projects already in
  early planning stages to respond.

  A phase-in approach has been used in several jurisdictions, including in the
  cities of Long Beach and San Jose, as described below:

-  The City of Long Beach phased in its inclusionary requirements over a three-
  year period, starting in 2021. Ownership projects that submitted their
  application for first approval in the first year were required to include 4
  percent of units as affordable to Moderate-Income households. Those applying
  in the second year had to include 5 percent of units as affordable, and those
  applying in the third year had to include 10 percent of units as affordable.
  Similarly, for rental projects, applicants in the first year had to include 5
  percent of units as affordable to Very-Low Income households, with the
  requirements increasing to 6 percent and then 11 percent for applicants in the
  second and third years. The City’s in-lieu fee levels were similarly phased in.

-  In San Jose, the City adopted its inclusionary housing ordinance in early
  2010 but delayed implementation until 2013. The City also added a market-
  based “trigger” to allow for earlier implementation if the housing market
  picked up more quickly than expected. Specifically, the ordinance could go
  into effect if at least 2,500 building permits were issued within a 12-month
  consecutive period.

3. Adjust the housing requirements so that the complying projects
  automatically qualify for the State Density Bonus (SDB). As written, the
  City’s inclusionary requirement for for-sale projects qualifies developers for a
  10 percent density bonus through the SDB. For rental projects, the City’s
  current inclusionary requirements do not automatically align with
  requirements for using the SDB. However, if the City increases the current
  requirement of 9 percent of units for Low Income households to 10 percent of
  units, projects would automatically qualify for a 20 percent density bonus. The
  City could potentially eliminate the requirement for Moderate-Income housing
  on rental to offset the cost of the additional Low-Income requirement. While
  this adjustment to the rental inclusionary requirements may not completely
  resolve feasibility concerns under current market conditions, the additional
  density and other regulatory waivers and concessions allowed under the SDB
  have economic value and can improve the feasibility of a residential project.

4. Consider adopting an in-lieu fee that is lower than the equivalent
  subsidy of providing units on-site. This would lessen the cost burden on
  developers while still generating revenue for City to use specifically for
  affordable housing initiatives and opportunities. Some examples of cities that
  have implemented such a strategy include Jurupa Valley and San Clemente.

  In taking this approach, the City should anticipate that most developers will
  choose to pay the in-lieu fee. However, even under this approach, some
  developers may still choose to build affordable units on-site anyway to qualify
  for the extra density and the waivers/concessions available under the SDB,
  which may be even more valuable to their project.

  If the City does take this approach, it may still only be helpful to the
  developers of attached townhome projects under current market conditions.
  Given the feasibility challenges demonstrated for multifamily development at
  market rates, even an in-lieu fee that is set below the equivalent cost of the
  on-site inclusionary requirement (e.g., $2 to $5 per square foot) may be more
  cost than new projects of this type can absorb at this time.

  It is also important to note that while cities do not often take this approach at
  the outset of establishing a new inclusionary housing program, it tends to
  happen over time if cities do not regularly update their inclusionary housing
  in-lieu fees. For example, cities that have not updated their in-lieu fees in
  some time may find that the cost to a developer of complying with the
  inclusionary requirement by building affordable units on-site far exceeds the
  cost of paying the in-lieu fee, given changes in development costs over time.

While the above strategies will not change the market and economic conditions
impacting residential development projects, they can reduce the additional costs
associated with inclusionary requirements. This in turn may increase the
likelihood that any individual market-rate project can feasibly contribute to the
supply of affordable units in the City.

 SUBJECT:  Adopt a Ordinance Establishing a Business License Tax Schedule

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Adopt an urgency ordinance establishing a business license tax schedule;
  2. Introduce and waive first reading of an ordinance establishing a business license
  tax schedule;
  3. Approve a one-time extension for renewal of business license tax, due and
  payable by April 1, 2025; and
  4. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

CEQA (California Environmental Quality Act):
These actions are exempt from review under the California Environmental Quality Act
(California Public Resources Code §§ 2100, et seq., “CEQA”) and CEQA regulations (14
California Code of Regulations §§ 15000, et seq.) because they establish rules and
procedures to implement government funding mechanisms; do not involve any
commitment to a specific project which could result in a potentially significant physical
impact on the environment; and constitute an organizational or administrative activity that
will not result in direct or indirect physical changes in the environment. Accordingly,
neither of the propositions constitute a “project” that requires environmental review (see
specifically 14 CCR § 15378(b)(4-5)).

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
On November 5, 2024, voters adopted Measure BE which updated the structure of the
City’s business license tax to be based on a business’s gross receipts. The measure was
adopted based upon a 70.46% voter approval.

In order to continue to be an attractive place for larger businesses to operate, City staff is
recommending a scaled business license tax (BLT) schedule for businesses earning over
$25,000,000 annually. The City is also seeking approval for one-time extension for
renewal of business license tax, due and payable by April 1, 2025.

BACKGROUND:

  Page 91 of 394
 Staff Report
Page 2 of 3
December 18, 2024

Like many cities, the City of Monterey Park imposes a local business tax to help fund
municipal services within the community. The City uses these revenues for City services
such as police patrol, fire suppression, parks, recreation, maintenance services, library
services and senior programs. The business license tax is not regulatory; it is for revenue
generation only.

The Monterey Park Municipal Code (“MPMC”) § 5.08.010 requires that any person (which
includes businesses) owning or transacting business in the City must obtain a license,
regardless of where the business is physically located.

Approximately seven of the current 4,700 businesses within the City are estimated to
gross over $25,000,000 in revenue annually. The next highest revenue grossing business
earns less than $10,000,000 annually. City staff is proposing to adopt a Resolution
allowing for a scaled BLT schedule that would ensure fairness while remaining business-
friendly to the seven extremely high grossing businesses. The Resolution permits an
automatic annual increase based on the Consumer Price Index (CPI) for All Urban
Consumers for the prior 12-month period ending on October 31st and would be applied
and effective on Janaury1st of each year (beginning January 1, 2026). Section 9 of
Measure BE authorizes the City Council to implement the BLT via regulations adopted by
ordinance.

To ensure that the City may collect the BLT on schedule, it is recommended that the City
adopt the draft urgency ordinance that would take effect immediately. This would allow
the City to begin collecting the BLT on January 1, 2025. Furthermore, Municipal Code §
5.08.210, states annual business license tax shall be due and payable in advance on the
first day of January of each year. To allow businesses to adjust to the new BLT structure,
the City is seeking approval for a one-time extension for renewal of business license tax,
due and payable by April 1, 2025.

2024-25 STRATEGIC PLAN GOAL:
With the passing of Measure BE, the City is seeking to achieve its goal of maintaining
fiscal stability of our City’s financial resources, specifically its objective of reviewing and
revising city revenue sources while also maintaining a business-friendly climate and
ensuring an equitable, fair, and modern business license tax base. Setting a BLT
Schedule will allow businesses grossing $25,000,000 or more annually to pay their fair
share without unduly impacting their overall operations and will help the City maintain
fiscal stability.

FISCAL IMPACT:
The City currently receives approximately $800,000 in BLT. The passing of Measure
BE inclusive of the business license tax schedule is expected to generate approximately
$1,200,000 annually for the city in general fund revenues, an increase of $400,000.

STREET CLASSIFICATIONS

Each of these segments is classified and defined with roadway classifications as listed in the
California Road Systems (CRS) Maps that are approved by the Federal Highway Administration
and maintained by the Department of Transportation (CVC 40802). Functional classifications are
used in determining which type of roads are eligible for Federal funding to maintain the roads.
Usually Principal Arterials, Secondary Arterial and Major Collectors are eligible.

Functional classification is the process by which streets and highways are grouped into classes, or
systems, according to the character of service they are intended to provide. Basic to this process
is the recognition that individual roads and streets do not serve travel independently in any major
way. Rather, most travel involves movement through a network of roads. Functional classification
defines how a particular road or street plays in serving the flow of trips through a highway network.
The four functional systems for urbanized areas are urban principal arterials, minor arterials, major
collectors, and local roads.

Principal Arterial: Principal Arterials carry most of the trips entering and leaving the City as well as
serves the major centers of activity of a City, carries the highest traffic volume along its corridors
while carrying the major portion of trips entering and leaving the urban area.

Secondary Arterial: The secondary arterial street system includes all arterials not classified as
principal and contains facilities that place more emphasis on land access than the higher system

and offer a lower level of traffic mobility. Such facilities may carry local bus routes and provide
intra-community continuity, but ideally should not penetrate identifiable neighborhoods. This
system should include urban connections to rural collector roads where such connections have
not been classified as urban principal arterials.

Collector: The collector street system provides both land access service and traffic circulation
within residential neighborhoods, commercial and industrial areas. It differs from the arterial system
in that facilities on the collector system may penetrate residential neighborhoods, distributing trips
from the arterials through the area to the ultimate destination. Conversely, the collector street also
collects traffic from local streets in residential neighborhoods and channels it into the arterial
system.

Local: These roadways provide direct access to individual residential properties, schools, and
churches typically with a posted speed of 25 MPH. Through traffic on local streets are usually
discouraged. Local roads within residential and business district zones are not subject to Speed
Trap provisions and are posted at the Prima Facie speed limit. Service to through traffic movement
is usually deliberately discouraged.

SECTION 2: OVERVIEW

CALIFORNIA VEHICLE CODE:

Speed limits in California are governed by the California Vehicle Code (CVC), Sections 22348
through 22413. The statutes establish or provide means of establishing speed limits by:

1. Basic speed limit law.
  Section 22350 of the CVC provides that no person shall drive a vehicle upon a highway at a
  speed greater than is reasonable or prudent having due regard for weather, visibility, traffic
  and the surface and width of the highway, and in no event at a speed which endangers the
  safety of persons or property. This is the basic speed limit law.

2. Prima facie speed limits are specified by statute or established by the State or local authorities
  within their respective jurisdictions on the basis of an engineering and traffic survey. Prima facie
  speed limits are specific limits stated in the CVC or specific limits established on the basis of an
  engineering and traffic survey authorized by the CVC. Prima facie speed limits are preempted
  by the basic speed limit law when the conditions in CVC Section 22350 are met.

  Section 22352 of the CVC establishes prima facie speed limits as follows and shall be
  applicable unless changed as authorized in the CVC and if so changed, only when signs have
  been erected giving notice of the change:

  a. Fifteen miles per hour.
  • At a railroad grade crossing with an obstructed view.
  • At an uncontrolled highway intersection with an obstructed view.
  • In an alley.

  b. Twenty-five miles per hour.
  • On any highway other than a State highway, in any business or residence district, CVC
  Sections 235 and 515 define a "business district” and a “residence district” respectively.
  Section 240 and 40802 of the CVC prescribes a method for determining whether a
  highway can be considered within a business or residence district.
  • Unless a different limit is established by procedures described elsewhere in the code.
  • In a school zone, posted with SCHOOL warning signs.
  • When passing a facility primarily used by senior citizens and contiguous to a street other
  than a State highway and posted with a SENIOR warning sign.

Sections 22357 and 22358 of CVC authorize local authorities to establish prima facie speed limits

SPEED TRAP:

Section 40802 2B(i) of the CVC provides that prima facie speed limits established under Sections
22352, 22354, 22357, 22358 and 22358.3 may not be enforced by radar unless the speed limit has
been justified by an engineering and traffic survey conducted within one of the following time
periods; five years to the date of the violation, within the last 7 years or if an engineering and traffic
survey was conducted more than 7 years prior to the date of the alleged violation, and a
registered engineer evaluates the section of the highway and determines that no significant
changes in roadway or traffic conditions have occurred, including, but not limited to, changes in
adjoining property or land use, roadway width, or traffic volume, the survey applies for 14 years.

This section does not apply to local streets, roads, school zones or senior zones which have been
set at the Prima Facie speed limit. Local streets are defined to have the following characteristics:
  • Width not more than 40 feet
  • Not more than .5 miles of uninterrupted length
  • 1 lane in each direction

primarily used by senior citizens or the grounds thereof that is posted with a standard “Senior”
warning sign pursuant to Section 22352.

ENGINEERING AND TRAFFIC SURVEY:

Section 627 of CVC defines the term engineering and traffic survey and lists its requirements.
Section 627 states: "An engineering and traffic survey shall include, among other requirements
deemed necessary by the Department of Transportation, consideration of all of the following:
prevailing speeds as determined by traffic engineering measurements, accident records,
highway traffic and roadside conditions not readily apparent to the driver."

The Engineering and Traffic Survey should contain sufficient information to document that the
conditions of CVC Section 627 have been complied with and that other conditions not readily
apparent to motorists are properly identified.

In determining the speed limit, which most appropriately facilitates the orderly movement of traffic
and is reasonable and prudent, crucial factors such as prevailing speeds, unexpected conditions,
and collision records are examined.

Determination of posted speed limits follow the latest CAMUTCD Policy as Revision 7 March 2023
by the State of California Department of Transportation. Speed limits shall be established at the
nearest 5 mph increment of the 85 th percentile speed of free-flowing traffic (CVC Section
22358.6(a)). However, in cases in which the speed limit needs to be rounded up to the nearest
five miles per hour increment of the 85th percentile speed, the Department of Transportation or a
local authority may decide to instead round down the speed limit to the lower five miles per hour
increment, but then the Department of Transportation or a local authority shall not reduce the
speed limit any further for any reason CVC 21400(4)(b).

An example of the application of this speed limit criteria is as follows:
  • If the 85th percentile speed in a speed survey is (37 MPH) then the speed limit would be
  posted at 35 MPH or optionally reduced to 30 MPH. However,
  • If the 85th percentile speed in a speed survey is (38 MPH) then the speed limit would be
  posted at 40 MPH or optionally reduced to 35 MPH.

The 85th percentile speed is often referred to as the critical speed. Pace speed is defined as the
10-mile increment of speed containing the largest number of vehicles. Speed limits established on
the basis of the 85th percentile conform to the consensus of those who drive highways as to what
speed is reasonable and prudent and are not dependent on the judgment of one or a few
individuals.

Basic speed law states that no person shall drive at a speed greater than is reasonable or prudent.
The majority of drivers comply with this law. Speed limits set at the 85 th percentile speed provide
law enforcement officers with a means of controlling drivers who will not conform to what the
majority considers reasonable and prudent.

The fundamentals used to establish speed limits recognize that the majority of drivers behave in a
safe and reasonable manner but need to be advised of conditions which may not be readily
apparent. For this reason, collision history, roadway conditions, traffic characteristics, and land
use, must be analyzed along with speed measurements to determine speed limits. Speed limit
changes are usually coordinated with visible changes in roadway conditions or roadside
developments.

In general, speed limits cannot be successfully enforced without voluntary compliance by a
majority of drivers. Consequently, only the driver whose behavior is clearly out of line with the
normal flow of traffic is considered a violator for enforcement purposes.

The radar equipment used to collect speed measurements was a SCOUT-MPH Traffic Radar, SHD-
04287 serial number, manufactured by Decatur. The unit was calibrated before each series of

The results of the radar speed measurements were computed, analyzed, and summarized on
standard Traffic Survey Forms. Significant values obtained from computations are as follows:

  •  The Critical Speed or 85th percentile speed, is the speed at or below which 85 percent of
  the traffic is moving. The Critical Speed is the primary guide in determining what the
  majority of drivers believe is safe and reasonable. Speed limits set higher than the Critical
  Speed are not considered reasonable and safe. The accepted practice is to set the speed
  limit at the nearest 5 MPH increment to the Critical Speed or 85th percentile speed unless
  other factors require a lower limit.

  •  The 5 or 10 MPH pace is a measure of the dispersion of speeds within the survey sample
  and is that 5 or 10 MPH increment containing the highest percentage of speeds in the total
  sample. The accepted practice is to keep the speed limit within the 10 MPH pace after
  considering the Critical Speed and any factors requiring a speed lower than the Critical
  Speed.

The Engineering and Traffic Survey summaries presented in this report illustrate the results of a
thorough evaluation of the data collected and provides a recommended speed limit for each
street segment surveyed. In each case, the recommended speed limit is consistent with the
prevailing behavior as demonstrated by the radar speed measurements.

The Legislature, in adopting Section 22358.5 of the California Vehicle Code, has made it clear that
it is their intent that physical conditions such as width, curvature, grade and surface conditions, or
any other condition readily apparent to a driver, in the absence of other factors, would not require
special downward speed zoning. The basic rule of Section 22350 is sufficient regulation as to such
conditions.

The recommendations contained in this report were intended to establish prima facie speed limits.
Prima Facie limits advise the motorist and enforcement agencies of the reasonable speed for a
section of highway for prevailing conditions. They are not intended to be absolute. All violations
of these speed limits are violations of the basic speed law (Section 22350 of California Vehicle
Code). This statute states that a person shall not drive a vehicle as a speed greater than is safe
having regard for traffic, roadway, and weather conditions. A prima facie limit merely suggests a
safe speed under normal conditions.

CEQA (California Environmental Quality Act):
This Ordinance is exempt from review under the California Environmental Quality Act
(California Public Resources Code §§ 21000, et seq., “CEQA”) and the regulations
promulgated thereunder (14 California Code of Regulations §§ 15000, et seq., the “CEQA
Guidelines”) because it consists only of minor revisions and clarifications to an existing
code of speed control regulations established in accordance with California law and will
not have the effect of deleting or substantially changing any regulatory standards or
findings. This Ordinance, therefore, is an action being taken for enhanced protection of
the environment and that does not have the potential to cause significant effects on the
environment. Consequently, it is categorically exempt in accordance with CEQA
Guidelines §§ 15301 as a minor alteration of existing public or private structures involving
no expansion of use; 15305 as a minor alteration in land use limitations which do not result
in any changes in land use or density; and 15308 as an action taken by a regulatory agency
as authorized by California law to assure maintenance or protection of the environment.

BOARD/COMMISSION REVIEW:

and reasonable speed limits 26 segments citywide, including its recommendations, to the
Traffic Commission on October 17, 2024. The Traffic Commission was informed that the

questions or concerns.

2.32.090: Determination of Appropriate Unit.
A. The policy objectives in determining the appropriateness of units regarding the effect of a
  proposed unit are:

  1. Efficient operations of the city and its compatibility with the primary responsibility of the city
  and its employees to effectively and economically serve the public; and

  2. Providing employees with effective representation based on recognized community of
  interest considerations.
  Page 248 of 394
 B. These policy objectives require that the appropriate unit shall be the broadest feasible grouping
  of positions that share an identifiable community of interest. Factors to be considered are:

  1. Similarity of the general kinds of work performed, types of qualifications required, and the
  general working conditions.

  2. History of representation in the city and in similar employment; except however, that no unit
  may be deemed to be an appropriate unit solely on the basis of the extent to which
  employees in the proposed unit have organized.

  3. Consistency with the organizational patterns of the city.

  4. Number of employees and classifications, and the effect on the administration of employer-
  employee relations because of the fragmentation of classifications and/or proliferation of
  units.

  5. Effect on the classification structure and impact on the stability of the employer-employee
  relationship because of dividing a single or related classification among two or more units.

C. Notwithstanding the foregoing provisions, managerial, supervisory, and confidential
  responsibilities, are determinative factors in establishing appropriate units hereunder.
  Therefore, such managerial, supervisory, and confidential employees may not represent any
  employee organization which represents other employees and may only be included in a unit
  consisting solely of managerial, supervisory, or confidential employees respectively.

2.32.100: Appeals.

A. An employee organization aggrieved by a determination of the Employee Relations Officer that
  a Recognition Petition, Challenging Petition, Decertification Petition, Determination of an
  Appropriate Unit, Unit Modification Petition, or Severance Request was not filed in compliance
  with this chapter may, within 10 calendar days of notice thereof, appeal such determination to
  the City Manager for final decision.

B. Appeals to the City Manager must be filed in writing with the City Clerk and a copy be provided
  to the Employee Relations Officer by the appellant. The written appeal must be received by the
  City Clerk no later than 10 calendar days after the Employee Relations Officer sent a decision.
  An employee organization’s appeal must state the complete basis for the appeal and be
  confined to a determination of whether or not the unit resulting from the Employee Relations
  Officer’s decision was appropriate. The City Manager must issue a final written decision as to
  whether the Employee Relations Officer’s decision was appropriate. If the City Manager finds
  the decision was not appropriate, the City Manager will make the final decision.

C. The City Manager must conduct the appeal hearing within 15 calendar days after receiving the
  appeal and issue a written decision within 15 calendar days after conclusion of the hearing.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:

The City conducted a review of the Employee Relations section in the Monterey Park
Municipal Code (“MPMC”). This occurred after the California Public Employment
Relations Board (“PERB”) found that the City’s procedures for recognizing
associations/unions were insufficient for making an appropriate union designation. The
proposed changes to MPMC Chapter 2.32 provide the appropriate procedures and
processes to recognize or appeal new associations/unions. City representatives
discussed and reviewed the MPMC section modification with representatives from the
current recognized associations/unions. The association/union representatives had an
opportunity to meet and discuss the impacts of the revisions and the groups agreed with
the revisions. The proposed amendments to the MPMC provide processes and
procedures for associations recognition along with appeal and decertification procedures.

seq., “CEQA”) and CEQA Guidelines (14 California Code of Regulations §§ 15000, et

policies and procedure-making.

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Receiving and Filing the staff report summarizing the status of the emergency
  replacement of self-contained breathing apparatuses; and
  2. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

BACKGROUND:
On December 18, 2024, City Council adopted Resolution No. 2024-R98 authorizing the
City Manager to take necessary measures for the emergency replacement of self-
contained breathing apparatuses (“SCBA”) for the Fire Department. SCBAs are critical
personal protective equipment for fire suppression staff and the department’s current
inventory is no longer supported for repairs and replacement parts as of December 16,
2024. To ensure fire suppression staff are properly protected, the current inventory of
SCBAs needs immediate replacement.

Staff obtained a quote from Bauer Compressors, Inc. for the replacement of SCBAs,
which includes both the items and a comprehensive service warranty for $633,812.92.

The City ordered the replacement SCBAs from Bauer Compressors on December 19,
2024. The vendor provided a 60-day delivery timeline, with anticipated delivery in the
middle of February 2025. When the items are received, immediate training and calibration
will take place, and then the SCBAs will be deployed for use.

FISCAL IMPACT:
The project is being funded by the General Fund. The estimated cost of the project is
$635,000.
