SECTION 1 – APPROACH AND SCOPE OF WORK
Project Understanding
The Monterey Pass Road Complete Streets Project presents a new opportunity for
the City to provide interconnectivity between dense residential communities, schools
such as East Los Angeles Community College (ELAC), job centers, warehouses
along this corridor, and commercial areas further along Garvey Avenue and
Atlantic Avenue. The City of Monterey Park has been taking a proactive approach
to implementing its part of the 2014 San Gabriel Valley Regional Bicycle Master
Plan and elements of its 2024 Climate Action Plan to expand the pedestrian and
bike network. At the same time, the City has incorporated public priorities into their
roadway’s projects, including securing Los Angeles Metropolitan Transportation
Authority (LA Metro) funds for this project rather than on other corridors such as
  THE VISION
Atlantic Avenue. Through this project, the City wishes to implement bicycle facilities
and pedestrian sidewalk improvements along the corridor. These improvements  Together, we will transform the
are consistent with the San Gabriel Valley Bicycle Master Plan and Climate Action
Plan, providing access to transportation for those without personal vehicles, and  Monterey Pass Road into a safer,
promoting healthy communities. This important corridor runs parallel to the I-710  greener, and more active
and I-10 freeways and connects the northern and southern sections of the City.
A similar parallel route isn’t available until Atlantic Avenue, which is 1.2 miles to  community for ALL users.
the east. When traffic occurs on the parallel highways, Monterey Pass Road is
susceptible to cut-through traffic during daily rush hour, making this area not only
important for local mobility, but also for the regional network. These factors create
layers of complexity in a project that involves many modes of travel including
passenger vehicles, bicycles, pedestrians, commercial vehicles, and local Spirit Bus Transit Service.

The San Gabriel Valley Regional Bicycle Master Plan (Plan), adopted in 2014, identifies Monterey Pass Road as a corridor where enhanced,
physical buffered Class II bicycle lanes would be appropriate. It is important to note that the Class IV nomenclature was not in common use
when the Plan was written and is not used in the Plan; a physical buffered Class II bicycle lanes would now be referred to as a Class IV bicycle
lane. In the Plan, these lanes integrate with proposed Class II bicycle lanes along Floral Drive, connecting cyclists to ELAC. In the northern
area of the City, the Plan calls for Class III Bike Route along Garvey Avenue, providing access to downtown Monterey Park. Meanwhile, the
Downtown Linkages Plan suggests Class II Bike Lanes along Newmark Street, providing a safe parallel route to Garvey Avenue along with
sidewalk widening projects. All of these proposed improvements are important pieces for Monterey Park to meet its goals of increasing the
active transportation mode share and the proposed changes to Monterey Pass Road are an essential component of this vision.

The curb-to-curb width along the Monterey Pass Road project corridor stays consistent at 70 feet with an overall right-of-way width of 100 feet.
Parkway areas are 15 feet wide with some segments having four to six-foot sidewalks, while many areas lack sidewalks altogether. Additionally,
there is limited street lighting along the corridor, which is a safety concern for bikes and pedestrians. Identification of the project limits and
constraints can be seen in Exhibit 1: Project Location Map on the following page along with our approach to turning these challenges into
opportunities as outlined on pages 12-14.This cross-sectional diversity requires a thoughtful and creative approach to bicycle and pedestrian
facility design to upgrade the entire corridor to comply with Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) requirements. Another important factor to
consider is the land use along and surrounding the corridor. While the land use in the City’s General Plan is industrial, many of the areas nearby
are residential land uses that use the corridor for commuting. Today, numerous warehouses line the street, with over 180 entryways and driveways
along the corridor leading to many conflicts and access issues.Residents enter the corridor via streets like Vagabond Drive to access the I-710,
I-60, and East Los Angeles College Area to the south and Garvey Avenue and the City of Alhambra to the north. This means that Monterey Pass
Road contains a diverse mix of traffic including commuters, cut-through traffic, residents, and commercial trucks. Finally, many of the warehouses
along the corridor use the street for loading/unloading, which can block traffic flow. Any new street configuration will have to minimize these
potential conflicts and improve overall safety. Safety is paramount, conflicting movements between multiple modes of transportation needs to
be considered, and roadway design should to be purposeful. Our vision is to help the City develop a consistent design that balances pedestrian
access, vehicular traffic, bicycle mobility, bus operations, warehouse ingress and egress, and parking facilities within this constrained roadway.
The City needs a well-rounded team that can address this challenge with a cohesive design that establishes harmony among often competing
transportation modes. This process will incorporate technical knowledge, visionary creativity, and community collaboration to create a project that
the City will be proud to showcase for residents, businesses, and visitors.

Outreach will be based on our extensive experience, lessons learned, and local relationships built with the City. We will work together
to develop an informative and inclusive approach to community outreach, bolstered by the technical work produced by the planning and
engineering team. Our team will be tactful while considering the unique qualities and nuances of this roadway. We have experience conducting
outreach and presenting before City Council in Monterey Park through our San Gabriel Valley Feasibility Study and will bring the knowledge
and lessons learned from this work into the Monterey Pass Road Complete Streets Project. In this project, residents and business owners and
residents alike have expressed concerns including reducing traffic capacity to install bike lanes, more bike/pedestrian traffic and thus more
potential conflicts, business operations, connectivity to other bike lanes, and overall safety. Highlighting these topics in outreach materials and
meetings, including proposed solutions, will help the City build consensus on these issues with the public faster and streamline the process to

 Scope Control

have tailored our approach to project scopes and fees accordingly. A clearly defined scope and fee help so that the expectations of both the
agency and the Kimley-Horn project manager can be met, and projects can be delivered more efficiently.

Part Three. Regular monitoring and updating of a project work plan, which is created at the start of each project. The project work plan is tailored
to the specific type and size of the project and includes basic information such as project scope, budget, and schedule as well as additional
project-specific items such as document control, quality control/quality assurance (QC/QA), risk management, staffing, and communication plans.

Our traffic engineers have developed and produced thousands of signing and striping plans across California. We strive to develop striping

are extremely familiar with documents that assist with the preparation of striping plans, including the California Manual on
Uniform Traffic Control Devices (CA MUTCD) and the Federal Highway Administration and NACTO guidelines for pedestrian and
bicycle devices.

Street Lighting
Kimley-Horn has performed street lighting analysis and design using the Federal Roadway Lighting Handbook standards to address street
lighting and parking/area lighting across the country. Kimley-Horn staff are thoroughly experienced with incorporating the requirements,
such as the current National Electric Code, that govern the installation of electrical conduit into our designs. Our engineers bring a local
understanding of the coordination with local utilities and power services. Key services provided by our engineers include roadway lighting
and design outdoor lighting applications, and lighting protection design. Appropriate lighting—both aesthetically and functionally—can help
provide clarity of directional cues for cars, bicyclists, and pedestrians.

  Traffic Safety
Kimley-Horn provides comprehensive traffic safety services including local road safety plans (LRSPs), systemic safety evaluations, road safety
audits, safe routes to school, project and grant development, vision zero strategies, and other focused studies to help reduce traffic injuries
and fatalities in California. Additionally, Kimley-Horn is the lead consultant for Caltrans’ Strategic Highway Safety Plan and is helping to direct
statewide safety improvement priorities as indicated in the Highway Safety Improvement Program and other funding initiatives. Our team has
more registered Road Safety Professionals than any other firm in the country.

Kimley-Horn takes a proactive approach to safety analysis. We use historical collision data to identify roadway characteristics and driver
behaviors that are associated with injury and fatal crashes in a given city, county, or region. We then develop customized countermeasure
toolboxes to address those specific characteristics to aid in widespread funding and implementation. Our safety team works closely with
traffic operations, roadway design, and mobility planning teams to facilitate that safety improvements are combined with efforts to improve the
transportation system for all users. Our team has completed safety plans for dozens of agencies in California and is working on many more.

 City of Whittier, Pio Pico State Park Trail, Whittier, CA
Kimley-Horn provided design consulting services to the City of Whittier for a bicycle facility that connects Pio Pico Historic Park and the San

 City of Santa Clara, Benton Street Bikeway Planning Study, Santa Clara, CA
Kimley-Horn, as a subconsultant, was selected by the City of Santa Clara to evaluate the traffic operations of the Benton Street Bikeway
project. This project seeks to install buffered bicycle lanes (Class IIB), bicycle boulevard (Class IIIB), and/or separate bikeways (Class IV) along
Benton Street between Dunford Way and Lincoln Street. As part of this work, some of the options will reduce the number of travel lanes along

counts, bicycle counts were collected for the weekday AM, weekday PM, weekday midday, and Saturday time periods. Traffic diversion
from the project options were determined using the City of Santa Clara’s travel demand model and post-processing modifications based on
engineering judgment. Intersection LOS and queuing were evaluated using Highway Capacity Manual (HCM) methodology within PTV Vistro
software. Travel times were evaluated using PTV VISSIM software.

organizations annually. Appointments are recommended by the Mayor and confirmed

District for a term of two years pursuant to Health and Safety Code §2024(a).

   Summary of Organizations

•  Board of Education/City Council Joint Use Committee (Alhambra Unified School
  District) is a joint committee to share ideas and discuss joint use efforts between the
  City and the Alhambra Unified District to promote safety and well-being of the children
  attending the schools in the City. Meetings: Varies.

•  California Contract Cities Association (CCCA) is a collection of member cities
  united for a common cause. The general purpose is to serve as a rallying point for
  cities contracting for municipal services to ensure constituents the best service at the
  minimum cost. Through municipal seminars, education, exchange of ideas and
  information, the association combines resources to influence policy decisions
  affecting its member cities. These cities band together to form a collective voice.
  Meetings: CCCA Board of Directors meetings are typically held on the third
  Wednesday of each month at 6:00 p.m. The location of meetings varies and rotates
  to member cities. More information, please visit: www.contractcities.org/.

•  Independent Cities Association (ICA) is made up of nearly 40 member cities in the
  Southern California area and focuses on public safety, education, infrastructure,
  legislative advocacy, intergovernmental relationships, and other major issues that
  transcend the boundaries of its member cities. ICA holds two Annual Seminars
  bringing together city council members, city officials and business partners for the
  purpose of collaboration, networking, and knowledge exchange. The Winter Seminar
  (held in January) addresses public safety and the Summer Seminar (held in July)
  focuses on contemporary issues. Meetings: 2nd Thursday. Meeting location
  varies. For more information about this organization, please visit: www.icacities.org/.

•  League of California Cities is an association of California city officials who work
  together to enhance their knowledge and skills, exchange information, and combine
  resources so that they may influence policy decisions that affect cities. The Los
  Angeles County Division is made up of 86 cities within Los Angeles County and
  provides members with the opportunity to exchange ideas and information and share
  the advantages of cooperative advocacy. The LA County Division holds general
  membership meetings at various times throughout the year. Meetings vary and
  details can be found at www.calcities.org/los-angeles-county-division. For more
  information about this organization, please visit www.cacities.org/.

•  Los Angeles County Sanitation District #2 is a public agency focused on converting
  waste into resources like recycled water, energy and recycled materials. The agency
  consists of 24 independent special districts serving about 5.6 million people in Los
  Angeles County. The service areas in the map below cover approximately 850 square
  miles and encompasses 78 cities and unincorporated areas in the county. The LA
  County Sanitation District #2 requires that the Mayor be the Council representative.
  The alternate representative has traditionally been the Mayor Pro Tem. Meetings are
  hybrid and are held on the 2nd Wednesdays at 1:30 p.m. and held at 1955
  Workman Mill Rd., Whittier and via Zoom. For more information about this
  organization, please visit, www.lacsd.org.

Updated: 11/14/2024  Page 387 of 394
 •  San Gabriel Valley Council of Governments (SGVCOG) is a joint powers authority
  made up of representatives from 30 cities, 3 Los Angeles County Supervisorial
  Districts, and the 3 Municipal Water Districts located in the San Gabriel Valley. The
  SGVCOG serves as a regional voice for its member agencies and works to improve
  the quality of life for the more than 2 million residents living in the San Gabriel Valley.
  The SGVCOG works on issues of importance to its member agencies, including
  transportation, homelessness, the environment, and water, and seeks to address
  these regionally. Meetings are held on the 3rd Thursday of each month at 4 p.m.
  at the SGVCOG Monrovia Office, 3rd Floor, 1333 S. Mayflower Ave, Suite #360,
  Monrovia. For more information about this organization, please visit www.sgvcog.org.

•  San Gabriel Valley Economic Partnership reflect the growing and broad
  membership including business, local government, colleges, and universities and non-
  profit organizations committed to the mission of advancing the economic vitality and
  quality of life of the San Gabriel Valley. Meeting dates and time vary. For more
  information about this organization, please visit www.sgvpartnership.org/.

•  San Gabriel Valley Mosquito & Vector Control District is a public health agency
  that provides ongoing mosquito and vector control from the San Gabriel Mountain
  foothills to the 26 cities in the San Gabriel Valley. Meetings are held on the 2nd
  Friday of each month at 7:00 a.m. at the District’s offices located at 1145 N.
  Azusa Canyon Road, West Covina. For more information about this organization,
  please visit www.sgvmosquito.specialdistrict.org.

•  Southern California Association of Governments (SCAG) is a Joint Powers
  Authority under California state law, established as an association of local
  governments and agencies that voluntarily convene as a forum to address regional
  issues. Under federal law, SCAG is designated as a Metropolitan Planning
  Organization (MPO) and under state law as a Regional Transportation Planning
  Agency and a Council of Governments. Regional Council meetings are hybrid and
  are held on the 1st Thursday of each month at 12:00-2:00 p.m. at the SCAG
  Offices located at 900 Wilshire Blvd. Ste. 1700, Los Angeles or via Zoom. For
  more information about this organization, please visit www.scag.ca.gov.

•  LAX/Community Noise Roundtable was created in September 2000 to provide an
  interactive forum to address current aircraft noise issues associated with aircraft
  operations to, from and at Los Angeles International Airport. Membership of the
  Roundtable consists of local elected officials and staff, representatives of
  congressional offices, members of recognized community groups, the FAA, the
  airlines and LAWA. This forum provides a mechanism to identify and address noise
  concerns by recommending courses of action to LAWA, the FAA, or other responsible
  entity that could reduce noise over affected communities. The Roundtable currently
  meets on the 3rd Wednesday of every odd numbered month and may schedule
  additional meetings as needed and held via video conference until further
  notice. For more information about this organization, please visit www.lawa.org/lawa-
  environment/noise-management/lawa-noise-management-lax/community-noise-
  roundtable.

  A RESOLUTION OF THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF MONTEREY

  BE IT RESOLVED by the Council of the City of Monterey Park as follows:

SECTION 1: The City Council finds as follows:

  A. Human trafficking is a public health issue and crime that exploits the most vulnerable
  among us and weakens the health and well-being of individuals, families, and
  communities across generations.

  B. An estimated 27.6 million people are subjected to human trafficking globally, including
  cases of human trafficking reported in every U.S. state and territory.

  C. Human trafficking can happen to anyone, but certain populations are
  disproportionately at risk, including people affected by abuse, violence, poverty,
  unstable living situations, social disconnection, or discrimination.

  D. People can be trafficked in person and online; in industries such as restaurants,
  domestic work, construction, agriculture, and factories; and by strangers or someone
  they know, including employers, partners, and family members.

  E. Human trafficking can be prevented by building individual, community, and societal
  understanding and resilience, reducing social inequities, and addressing the
  conditions that contribute to exploitation.

  F. Promoting awareness is crucial to the prevention and elimination of human trafficking
  within our City and an informed community is better equipped to identify and report
  instances of human trafficking, support victims, and collaborate with law enforcement
  agencies and non-profit organizations.

  G. A successful response to human trafficking requires a coordinated, community-wide
  effort and the City of Monterey Park is dedicated to ensuring anyone impacted by
  human trafficking can receive services that provide individualized care, understand
  the impact of trauma, and incorporate cultural and linguistic needs.

  H. The City of Monterey Park takes proactive steps to prevent and address human
  trafficking by providing important information and resources to residents about their
  rights, and works with local and regional non-profit organizations, government
  agencies and community based groups to provide resources, including mental health
  and wellness support, legal services, food assistance, peer support, vaccinations and
  screenings, and public benefit enrollment to at-risk populations.

  Page 393 of 394
   I. The City Council of Monterey Park hereby recognizes January 2025 as National
  Human Trafficking Prevention Month and encourages all residents, businesses,
  schools, and community organizations to participate in events, educational programs,
  and initiatives aimed at raising awareness about human trafficking and supporting
  efforts to combat it.

2-B.  DISCUSSION OF FINDINGS ON CITY’S UPDATED INCLUSIONARY HOUSING
  ORDINANCE FEASIBILITY/FEE STUDY

  On September 6, 2023, the City Council adopted an Inclusionary Housing
  Ordinance ("IHO”) and an in-lieu fee formula to encourage affordable housing in
  Monterey Park. The Council also directed the City Manager to assess the IHO’s
  financial feasibility and recommend in-lieu fees where necessary. To assist in this
  evaluation, the City partnered with the San Gabriel Valley Council of Governments
  (“SGVCOG”) and engaged Economic & Planning Systems (“EPS”) for a tailored
  feasibility study.

  On January 17, 2024, the feasibility study was presented to City Council and found
  that the IHO's requirements could present financial challenges for new residential
  projects, particularly smaller and mid-sized developments. Based on this analysis,
  the City Council directed staff to pause enforcement of the IHO for one year and
  revisit its financial feasibility in the coming year.

  EPS was hired to review the previously prepared feasibility study and update it to
  reflect current market conditions. In updating the feasibility study, during the
  Council-directed IHO enforcement pause, EPS looked at both direct and indirect
  factors that may change the financial feasibility of implementing the IHO. The
  study’s overall conclusion states that while the requirements of the IHO are likely
  to remain financially challenging for new residential development within the City
  and may constrain new projects, current market conditions have demonstrated
  improved feasibility of new residential projects overall since the previous analysis.

  Discussion: Director of Community Development Serrano and Planning Manager
  Chow introduced Senior Associate Chinmay Damle and Principal Julie Cooper
  from Economic and Planning Systems Inc. (EPS) to present the City’s feasibility
  study.

  Senior Associate Damle and Principal Cooper from EPS presented a PowerPoint
  Presentation about the City’s Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (IHO) feasibility
  study and provided potential options of consideration to the City Council.

  Action Taken: The City Council received and filed the report and presentation and
  provided direction to staff to as follows: temporarily pause the IHO requirements
  for at least 9 months - 12 months and return to City Council with an updated
  financial feasibility study for consideration by the Council in December or January
  (2026). During this pause, Staff is directed to (1) adjust the requirements of IHO
  relating to projects automatically qualifying for the State Density Bonus and (2) the
  adoption of an in-lieu fee at a level that is higher or equivalent of providing units
  on-site.

3-D.  CONSIDERATION AND POSSIBLE ACTION TO WAIVE SECOND READING OF

  CHAPTER 2.32 UPDATING EMPLOYEE RELATIONS

  The City conducted a review of the Employee Relations section in the Monterey
  Park Municipal Code (“MPMC”). This occurred after the California Public
  Employment Relations Board (“PERB”) found that the City’s procedures for
  recognizing associations/unions were insufficient for making an appropriate union
  designation. The proposed changes to MPMC Chapter 2.32 provide the
  appropriate procedures and processes to recognize or appeal new
  associations/unions. City representatives discussed and reviewed the MPMC
  section modification with representatives from the current recognized
  associations/unions. The association/union representatives had an opportunity to
  meet and discuss the impacts of the revisions and the groups agreed with the
  revisions. The proposed amendments to the MPMC provide processes and
  procedures for associations recognition along with appeal and decertification
  procedures.

  On December 18, 2024, City Council adopted Resolution No. 2024-R98
  authorizing the City Manager to take necessary measures for the emergency
  replacement of self-contained breathing apparatuses (“SCBA”) for the Fire
  Department. SCBAs are critical personal protective equipment for fire suppression
  staff and the Department’s current inventory is no longer supported for repairs and
  replacement parts as of December 16, 2024. To ensure fire suppression staff are
  properly protected, the current inventory of SCBAs needs immediate replacement.

  Staff obtained a quote from Bauer Compressors, Inc. for the replacement of
  SCBAs, which includes both the items and a comprehensive service warranty for
  $633,812.92.

  The City ordered the replacement SCBAs from Bauer Compressors on December
  19, 2024. The vendor provided a 60-day delivery timeline, with anticipated delivery
  in the middle of February 2025. When the items are received, immediate training
  and calibration will take place, and then the SCBAs will be deployed for use.
